Heading to Norway? These Are the Aircraft to Look Out For

by Matt Falcus 1 day ago
written by Matt Falcus 1 day ago 66 views
0 comments 0FacebookTwitterLinkedinRedditWhatsappEmail
66

Summary

  • Widerøe De Havilland Canada DHC-8
  • Royal Norwegian Air Force Lockheed C-130J Hercules
  • SAS Airbus A321LR
  • Norwegian Air Shuttle Boeing 737 MAX 8
  • North Sea Offshore Helicopters
  • Preserved Airliner Highlights

    • Royal Norwegian Air Force Boeing P-8A Poseidon
    • Norwegian Air Ambulance Aircraft

Instaread

Norway is one of Europe’s most fascinating countries for aviation enthusiasts. With its dramatic fjords, mountainous terrain, remote coastal communities and far-flung Arctic settlements, aviation plays an essential role in keeping the country connected.

For plane spotters, this creates some particularly interesting opportunities. While the main airports at Oslo, Bergen, Stavanger and Trondheim see plenty of familiar Airbus and Boeing airliners, Norway is also home to some unusual aircraft types, specialist operations and aviation museums that make it well worth exploring.

Perhaps the biggest attraction is the country’s network of small regional airports, many of which are served by turboprop aircraft that are becoming increasingly rare elsewhere in Europe. Add in offshore helicopters supporting the North Sea oil and gas industry, military transports, long-haul narrowbody jets and some fascinating preserved airliners, and there’s plenty to keep enthusiasts occupied.

You Might Be Interested In
  • Plane Spotting Challenge – Trip Report #10 – On Top of the World
  • Which Airlines Still Fly Classic Dash 8s?

Here are some of the aircraft and aviation highlights you should look out for on your next visit to Norway.

 

Widerøe De Havilland Canada DHC-8

Wideroe DH-8 100/200 line up at Trondheim

One of the biggest attractions for enthusiasts visiting Norway is the fleet of De Havilland Canada DHC-8 aircraft operated by Widerøe. While the larger Dash 8-Q400 is familiar across Europe, the airline’s smaller Dash 8-100 and -200 variants are becoming increasingly unusual and are among the most interesting aircraft to fly on in Norway.

These 39-seat turboprops are perfectly suited to Norway’s network of short-runway airports, many of which have runways of only around 800 metres. They connect small coastal communities and remote towns with larger regional centres, often making several stops on a single journey.

Bodø, Tromsø, Trondheim and Bergen are excellent starting points for finding these aircraft, while smaller airports such as Leknes, Svolvær, Sandnessjøen, Hammerfest and Mehamn offer some spectacular scenery and interesting approaches. Widerøe also operates the larger Dash 8-300, Q400 and a small fleet of Embraer E190-E2 jets.

For enthusiasts, flying aboard a Dash 8-100 or -200 into one of Norway’s tiny coastal airports is an experience not to be missed.

Royal Norwegian Air Force Lockheed C-130J Hercules

Norway’s military aviation scene is also worth investigating, particularly the Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules transport aircraft operated by the Royal Norwegian Air Force.

These four-engined turboprops are operated by 335 Squadron, based at Gardermoen Military Air Station, adjacent to Oslo’s main international airport. The military facilities share the airport’s runways, meaning enthusiasts watching arrivals and departures at Oslo Gardermoen may occasionally see a Hercules among the regular passenger traffic.

The aircraft undertake a variety of transport missions, including moving personnel and equipment, supporting military operations and humanitarian assignments. Although sightings are less predictable than scheduled airline movements, the distinctive sound and appearance of a Hercules make it a particularly welcome addition to a day’s spotting at Oslo.

SAS Airbus A321LR

Scandinavian Airlines operates a small fleet of Airbus A321LR aircraft, a long-range variant of the familiar A321neo capable of operating intercontinental routes with a narrowbody airliner.

These aircraft have been used on transatlantic services from Scandinavia, including Oslo to New York, allowing SAS to serve routes where a larger widebody aircraft might not be economical.

For plane spotters, the A321LR is an interesting aircraft to identify among the many standard A320-family jets operating around Oslo Gardermoen. Its longer range, additional fuel capacity and premium long-haul cabin distinguish it from the regular A321neo.

As SAS adjusts its long-haul network, it is worth checking current schedules to establish which services are operated by the A321LR rather than the airline’s larger Airbus A330 and A350 aircraft.

Norwegian Air Shuttle Boeing 737 MAX 8

Norwegian Air Shuttle is one of the most prominent airlines at Norway’s airports, operating a large fleet of Boeing 737 aircraft on domestic and European services.

Alongside its established Boeing 737-800 fleet, the airline has been steadily expanding its Boeing 737 MAX 8 operation. By the end of September 2026, Norwegian had 39 MAX 8 aircraft in its fleet, with further deliveries planned as part of a major fleet renewal programme.

Although the MAX is increasingly common worldwide, Norway is an excellent place to photograph Norwegian’s aircraft, particularly at Oslo, Bergen, Trondheim, Stavanger and Tromsø.

Another attraction is the airline’s distinctive tail-fin portraits, celebrating famous figures from Norwegian and wider Scandinavian history and culture. Spotters can enjoy identifying the different personalities as aircraft arrive and depart.

North Sea Offshore Helicopters

Peter Bakema (GFDL 1.2 or GFDL 1.2), via Wikimedia Commons

Norway’s enormous offshore oil and gas industry creates some of Europe’s most interesting helicopter operations.

Airports such as Bergen Flesland, Stavanger Sola, Florø and Hammerfest are important bases for helicopters carrying workers and supplies to offshore installations in the North Sea and Norwegian Sea.

Among the main operators are Bristow Norway and CHC Helicopter Service, with the Sikorsky S-92 being particularly prominent. Lufttransport also operates offshore helicopter services, including the Leonardo AW139, with the larger AW189 planned to join its operations.

Bergen is an especially interesting location, with Equinor reporting approximately 5,000 offshore helicopter flights annually from Flesland. Unlike many airports where helicopters are occasional visitors, these large twin-engined machines form a regular part of the daily traffic.

Preserved Airliner Highlights

Braathens Fokker F28 LN-SUC & Norving BN 2A Islander

Norway also has an impressive aviation heritage, with several museums preserving aircraft that played important roles in the country’s civil and military aviation history.

One of the most interesting is the Norwegian Aviation Museum at Bodø. Among its civil aircraft collection is a preserved Fokker F28 Fellowship, representing the type that helped bring regional jet travel to Norway. The museum also has an extensive military aircraft collection.

Braathens DC-6 LN-SUB

At Stavanger Sola, the Flyhistorisk Museum Sola is home to a magnificent Douglas DC-6B displayed in the colours of Braathens SAFE. The aircraft, formerly registered LN-SUB, returned to Norway from Alaska in 2020 and is displayed outside the museum, providing a wonderful reminder of Norway’s early post-war airline industry.

Another highlight is the former SAS Sud Aviation Caravelle Finn Viking, preserved inside the Norwegian Museum of Science and Technology in Oslo. The aircraft represents the early jet age of Scandinavian Airlines, which introduced the Caravelle in 1959. Visitors can now explore its passenger cabin and cockpit.

Norwegian Armed Forces DC-3

Finally, the Norwegian Armed Forces Aircraft Collection at Gardermoen is worth investigating for its preserved military aircraft, including types that served during the Cold War.

Together, these collections make Norway a rewarding destination for anyone interested in classic aircraft, as well as the modern airline scene.

Other Aircraft Worth Looking Out For

I would add three more aircraft categories to the main article. These offer something genuinely different, rather than simply listing every airline operating in Norway.

Royal Norwegian Air Force Boeing P-8A Poseidon

Norway’s strategic position on the northern edge of Europe makes maritime surveillance particularly important. The Royal Norwegian Air Force operates five Boeing P-8A Poseidon aircraft, based at Evenes Air Station in northern Norway.

Based on the Boeing 737-800 airliner, the P-8 is equipped with sophisticated surveillance equipment and is used to monitor maritime activity across the Norwegian Sea and North Atlantic.

Although military movements are unpredictable, Evenes shares its runways with the civilian Harstad/Narvik Airport, making it an interesting location for enthusiasts hoping to see one of these distinctive military derivatives of the Boeing 737.

Norwegian Air Ambulance Aircraft

Teemu Pesonen (GFDL 1.2 or GFDL 1.2), via Wikimedia Commons

Another interesting feature of Norway’s aviation scene is its extensive air ambulance network, which provides vital medical transport services to remote communities across the country.

Avincis Aviation Norway operates Beechcraft King Air 250 turboprops, specially equipped to carry patients and medical personnel. These aircraft are particularly suited to Norway’s smaller airports and challenging operating conditions.

The operator also uses Cessna Citation Latitude jets for longer-range medical transport, including aircraft based at Oslo and Tromsø.

Leonardo AW101 SAR Queen Rescue Helicopters

Norway’s demanding coastline, mountains and Arctic waters require a substantial search-and-rescue capability. One of the most impressive aircraft involved is the Leonardo AW101, known locally as the SAR Queen.

Operated by the Royal Norwegian Air Force’s 330 Squadron, these large three-engined helicopters have replaced the veteran Westland Sea King in Norway’s rescue service.

They can be encountered at several bases around the country, including Sola, Bodø, Florø, Ørland, Rygge and Banak. Their striking red-and-white colour scheme and distinctive three-engine configuration make them particularly photogenic aircraft.

For helicopter enthusiasts, the SAR Queen is another excellent reason to explore Norway’s regional aviation scene.
